opus-5.5.text:
Well, one thing I think often gets lost in public discussion is that when people hear someone described as a "short timelines" forecaster, they imagine that person is confidently predicting AGI in, say, two or three years. But when you actually look at the distributions these forecasters put out, including people like Daniel, they're usually quite wide. The median might be fairly near, but there's a long right tail, with a substantial share of probability on it taking a decade or more, sometimes much longer.

So I think the right way to read these forecasts is not as point predictions but as statements of deep uncertainty that happen to have a lot of mass early on. Someone might say their median is the late 2020s, and that sounds dramatic, but it also implies they think there's roughly a coin flip's chance it's later than that, and maybe a meaningful chance it's a lot later. Conversely, people with longer medians often still put non-trivial probability on things arriving soon. The distributions overlap far more than the headline numbers suggest.

That has a couple of implications. First, it's a mistake to treat the debate as "short timelines people versus long timelines people," as if one camp will be vindicated and the other refuted. If AGI arrives in 2035, that isn't really a refutation of someone whose median was 2028 but who had a fat tail. We should be judging forecasters on calibration over many questions, not on whether their median was hit.

Second, for decision-making, the shape of the distribution matters more than the median. If you take seriously a reasonable chance of very short timelines, that argues for some work that pays off quickly: preparing policy, building institutional capacity, doing safety work that's relevant to current systems. But the long tail means you shouldn't bet everything on that. You also want investments that pay off over a decade or two: training people, building fields, developing more fundamental research. A sensible portfolio hedges across the whole distribution rather than acting as if the median were certain.

And I'd add one more thing. These forecasts have tended to shift earlier over the last several years, which is itself informative. When the people who think hardest about a question keep updating in the same direction, that's a signal worth taking seriously, even while recognising that the uncertainty remains genuinely large.

r001.rationale: The response discusses wide distributions and medians but does not propose assessing uncertainty with the interval between the 10th and 90th percentiles.

r002.rationale: It says that short-timeline forecasters, including Daniel Kokotajlo, usually have wide distributions with substantial probability on much later arrival.

r003.rationale: It notes overlap among forecasts but does not say that very wide uncertainty intervals recur across different forecasting methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I've thought about a lot. I think the first thing to say is that it's genuinely to Daniel's credit that he puts numbers on things and makes his reasoning legible — the AI 2027 scenario, for example, isn't just a vibe, it's a worked-through story with explicit assumptions you can push on. That's much better than the vague "it's coming soon" or "it's decades away" that you often hear.

But when I look at the uncertainty in those forecasts, I try to separate a few different things. One is the stated uncertainty — someone like Daniel will give you a distribution, a median and tails, and you should take that seriously as his honest credence. The second is what I'd call the structural uncertainty, which is often much larger than the stated distribution captures. Almost all of these forecasts are built on an extrapolation of some trend — compute scaling, task-horizon doubling times, benchmark performance — and the trend is real, but the question is whether the thing being extrapolated actually bottoms out in the capability we care about. And that's a model uncertainty that doesn't show up neatly as wider error bars; it shows up as the whole forecast being somewhat off in a correlated way.

The third thing is that when someone's forecasts have been short for a while and then the dates get pushed out — which we've seen happen a bit, Daniel himself moved his median later — I think the right lesson isn't "he was wrong, ignore him." It's that the early-warning end of the distribution kept not arriving, and that's informative. You update, but you don't update all the way to complacency, because the underlying drivers are still there.

So my own view is that I'd put real probability mass on transformative AI within the next five years or so — enough that we should be acting as though it could happen — while thinking the median is probably somewhat further out than the shortest-timeline forecasters say. The key point, though, is that for decision-making, the shape of the distribution matters more than the median. If there's even a twenty or thirty percent chance that this happens by the end of the decade, that's an extraordinary situation, and most of what we should do follows from that tail rather than from arguing about whether the median is 2028 or 2035.

And I'd add one more thing: uncertainty here isn't just about the arrival date. It's about what "AGI" even means operationally. A lot of the disagreement between forecasters dissolves when you realise they're forecasting different thresholds. Daniel's talking about something like fully automated AI research; others are talking about broadly human-level economic labour; others about something more dramatic. So when I read a forecast, the first question I ask is "what event exactly is being forecast?" and the second is "what trend are you extrapolating, and what would have to be true for that trend to break?" If you can answer those, the stated uncertainty becomes much more interpretable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses medians, tails, and structural uncertainty, but does not propose using the 10th-to-90th-percentile interval to assess uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It identifies Daniel as a short-timeline forecaster and says he gives a distribution with a median and tails, but does not clearly characterize his forecast as broadly uncertain.

r003.rationale: It says forecasts commonly extrapolate trends, but does not observe that very wide uncertainty intervals recur across different forecasting methods.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to distinguish uncertainty about when AGI will arrive from disagreement about when it will arrive. You could have several people each quite confident in a particular date, but with very different dates. Or you could have people whose individual forecasts are themselves spread over decades. Those are different situations, even if you get the same average forecast.

With someone like Daniel Kokotajlo, I’d want to know how much probability he puts on longer timelines, rather than just hearing the date at the centre of his forecast. Having a short median timeline doesn’t necessarily mean being confident that AGI will arrive soon. It means putting half your probability before that point, and half after it. The other half could extend quite a long way out.

And the uncertainty cuts both ways. People sometimes treat uncertainty as a reason to dismiss short timelines. But if we’re uncertain, that can also mean there’s a meaningful chance of arrival earlier than we expect. For thinking about preparedness, that matters a great deal. We don’t need to settle on a single date before asking whether we’d be ready if it happened soon.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a forecast’s median and probability beyond it, but does not propose using the 10th-to-90th-percentile interval.

r002.rationale: It says a short median forecast could have a long tail and suggests checking Kokotajlo’s longer-timeline probability, but does not identify his forecast as actually expressing broad uncertainty.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that wide uncertainty intervals recur across different forecasting methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s helpful to distinguish uncertainty about when AGI will arrive from uncertainty about what happens after that. Someone might put a lot of probability on AGI arriving in the next few years, while still having quite a wide distribution over dates. Calling them a short-timelines forecaster can obscure that uncertainty.

And I’d want to ask what’s driving the forecast. Is it an extrapolation of recent progress? Is it a view about how much further scaling will take us? How much probability do they assign to encountering some obstacle that takes a long time to overcome? Those questions matter more than just the headline year.

With Daniel, I wouldn’t want to put words in his mouth about precisely how his uncertainty breaks down. But in general, I think we should take short timelines seriously without treating them as established. Uncertainty cuts both ways: it leaves room for things to take substantially longer, but it also means we can’t count on having that extra time. And for decisions about preparing for AGI, that possibility of an early arrival can be very important.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose assessing uncertainty with the interval between the 10th and 90th percentiles.

r002.rationale: It says a short-timelines forecast can have a wide date distribution, but explicitly avoids saying how Daniel Kokotajlo’s uncertainty breaks down.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that wide uncertainty intervals recur across different AGI forecasting methods.
